::: {.letter-metadata}
**Date:** May 20th [1871?][^1]  
**From:** Elderfield, Otterbourne, Winchester.  
**Manuscript:** MS Charlotte Mitchell
:::

My dear [Edith](people/person_749.qmd)
I should not think [Miss Adams](people/person_15.qmd) could have any objection to your girl. [^2]  She has one now whose [father](people/person_2270.qmd) is [Miss Sturges Bourne](people/person_1379.qmd)'s bailiff, and her [mother](people/person_1820.qmd) a ladys maid, the [girl](people/person_2269.qmd) is refined and more naturally ladylike looking than any of the others, but the sound is not much superior to yours.  I am going from home on Monday for a month but it can all be settled with Miss Adams, and I know she has room. I will prepare her before I go.  French comes naturally with her and is not an extra.[^3]

I was thinking of trying to drive over to see you when [Miss Seymour](people/person_1308.qmd) told me you were at Malvern.[^4] I suppose there is no chance of your being back in July, when [Margaret Roberts](people/person_1244.qmd) has promised me a visit, and I would try to bring her if she is pretty well.  A long drive always seems to me the most perfect way of enjoying a friend, one can talk without the sense of idleness, and with just distraction enough to offer variety if one wants it  Indeed I wish, as lookers on and sympathizers can not fail to wish that this serving by standing and waiting were not so very long and weary.[^5]  I still very much hope that force of time will bring more power, as it certainly does with many.  [Emily Awdry](people/person_81.qmd) who is the only one of the Moberlys I have seen, says her [father](people/person_1015.qmd) has felt this like the closing of cares and anxieties for his children, the thing he had cared to live for was the seeing [Selwyn](people/person_1026.qmd) launched.[^6]

If there be anything to write to me about this negotiation you had better direct here, as I shall be changing about a good deal

your affectionate
C M Yonge

---

[^1]: The year 1869 added in pencil in another hand, but it seems likely that the letter refers to Selwyn Moberly's death on 8 April 1871.
[^2]: Mary Adams (b.1831/2) ran a small boarding school in Otterbourne with her aunt from 1862.
[^3]: As far as this the text has been crossed through in pencil, as if part publication had been contemplated.
[^4]: Miss Seymour was probably Edith Jacob’s first cousin, daughter of  Rev. George Augustus Seymour (1828/9-1909), Rector of Holy Trinity, Winchester, whose wife Elizabeth Noel (d. 1868), was her aunt.
[^5]: John Milton, 'On His Blindness' 14: 'They also serve who only stand and wait.'  Edith Jacob was a confirmed invalid.
[^6]: The Moberlys' youngest son Selwyn died in 1871.
